title: Can Apps Teach You a Language?

blanks.sentence: Apps use _____ to test a recurring set of words.
App companies say many apps focus on language for _____ instead of directly teaching rules.
Children benefit from constant _____ to the language around them.
Research supports some direct teaching of _____ for adults.
For adults, matching a child's _____ is not realistic.
Adults may have only _____ each week to study a new language.
The _____ on exactly how well apps work remains limited.
One study compared two groups of _____ learning English.
In some _____, app learners improved a little more than classroom learners.
The expert wants more studies across apps, teaching approaches and _____.

multipleChoice.question: What similarity is suggested between many apps' stated approach and children's early language learning?
options: Both begin with formal grammar lessons before language use.
Both depend on a few hours of weekly homework.
Both can involve learning without direct explanations of rules.
Both provide the same amount of language exposure.

multipleChoice.question: What difference between child and adult learners does the expert emphasise?
options: Children receive more formal grammar lessons each week.
Adults already know the vocabulary of the new language.
Children use apps more often than adults can manage.
Children encounter the language much more continuously.

multipleChoice.question: Which activity best illustrates the direct teaching considered useful for adults?
options: A teacher explains a grammar rule to learners.
A learner repeats words without an explanation.
A child picks up speech from everyday surroundings.
An app presents situations without discussing rules.

multipleChoice.question: Why is a blend of app learning and direct teaching suggested for adults?
options: Apps make learning grammar impossible for adults.
Adults have limited exposure, while some direct teaching helps.
Classes recreate a child's constant language exposure.
Research has already found the exact best mix of methods.

multipleChoice.question: How did the two groups differ in the study's test results?
options: App learners led in some written grammar tests and appeared to lead in listening.
Classroom learners led in some written grammar tests and appeared to lead in listening.
App learners led in some written grammar tests; classroom learners appeared to lead in listening.
Classroom learners led in some written grammar tests; app learners appeared to lead in listening.

multipleChoice.question: What can be inferred from the expert's qualification of the study?
options: Similar outcomes may not hold for other apps and languages.
Neither group improved on any of the reported tests.
The learners studied for completely different lengths of time.
Written grammar results are never useful evidence.

multipleChoice.question: What role might platforms play alongside human teaching?
options: They might replace the teachers who explain rules.
They might recreate a child's full immersion.
They might remove the need for listening practice.
They might provide repeated practice with language.

multipleChoice.question: What approach follows from the final advice on improving different skills?
options: Use the app activity with the highest test score for every skill.
Combine app work with activities aimed at particular skills.
Replace apps entirely with podcasts and speaking partners.
Choose one method and use it for speaking, listening, reading and writing.
